newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Southeast Asian rubber seen downcast in near term.
newsitem.headline: Southeast Asian rubber seen downcast in near term.

text.p: Southeast Asia's rubber markets are expected to be fragile in the near term following news of high Thai stock levels but could bounce back on improved demand after the summer holiday season, traders said on Wednesday.

They also said that Thailand, the world's top rubber producer, would seek to boost its market share in Europe and the United States as the country's plan to increase output of rubber used in industrialised countries gathers speed.

The regional markets had been downcast since Monday after a Thai industry official told a regional gathering of producers on the tourist island of Bali over the weekend that the country had excess stocks of around 140,000 tonnes.
Traders who attended the meeting said the official had said about half the amount was in the hands of the private sector.
"We are already feeling the impact of the statement," one trader said. "Buyers have withdrawn from the market, and I expect prices to weaken through the week."
"But I am cautiously optimistic that prices will gain some strength when the summer holiday season is over and buyers begin to head back into the market," he added.

Traders said Indonesian rubber prices edged down on Wednesday on thin buying interest, while Singapore rubber futures were untraded in the morning session. A volatile Malaysian currency kept players sidelined as prices dipped.
Indonesian traders said they were puzzled over the Thai stock disclosure at a gathering where buyers were also present.
"Is there a hidden agenda for such market sensitive information to be made public, especially when buyers were present," one trader wondered. "The news has hit us."
"It is certainly a factor in the market, and buyers are taking advantage of the situation," he added.

Traders said the announement could be linked to Thailand's increased production of technically-specified rubber used by tyre-makers in Europe and the United States and the winding down of sheet rubber output shipped mostly to Japan and China.
"Thai rubber prices have to be attractive in order for them to be able to sell to Europe and the United States, which are traditional markets of Indonesia and Malaysia," one said.
"I think the process of switching from sheet rubber to technically specified rubber in Thailand is much faster than can be taken up by the U.S. and European markets," he added.
He said Thailand's buyers in China and Japan were not ready to absorb all of Bangkok's technically specified rubber, and so Thai players have to look to the United States and Europe.

"But I think it is only a matter of time before China's demand for technically specified rubber increases because as we know there are many multinationals which are setting up joint venture factories there," he added.
"Thailand is a newcomer to the technically specified rubber market and therefore its prices have to be competitive against rubber from Indonesia and Malaysia," he added.

Traders said producing technically specified rubber was a difficult process that needed years to perfect because it had to be made in accordance with tyre-makers' specifications which varied from one company to another.
